notes.meaning: The fifth angel blows his trumpet, signaling the start of the first great woe. John sees a star that had fallen from heaven to earth, representing a powerful angelic or spiritual figure. God permits this being to receive the key to the bottomless pit, showing that evil spirits are always subject to God's sovereign control.

differ.view: Older Baptist writers often saw the fallen star as a false religious ruler like the Pope or Muhammad, while many modern Baptists understand the star to be Satan cast out of heaven during the tribulation.

notes.meaning: The fallen star opens the bottomless pit, and a massive cloud of dark smoke pours out like the smoke of a great smelting furnace. This heavy black cloud rises so high and thick that the sun and the atmosphere are darkened. It portrays how demonic forces bring spiritual blindness, confusion, and moral ruin upon the world.

Out of the thick smoke comes a terrifying swarm of locusts that spreads across the earth. Unlike ordinary grasshoppers, these creatures receive power to inflict agony on people just like scorpions of the earth. They picture a horde of tormenting demons let loose upon an ungodly world.

God commands the demonic swarm not to harm grass, green plants, or trees, which are the normal food of natural locusts. Instead, they are permitted to strike only those human beings who lack the protective seal of God on their foreheads. This reveals that the Lord safely shields His own faithful people while allowing judgment to fall on the unrepentant.

differ.view: Some dispensational Baptists teach that the sealed people are strictly the 144,000 Jewish believers, while Reformed Baptists teach that the seal belongs to all the elect who trust in Christ.

notes.meaning: The locusts are strictly forbidden to take any human lives; their commission is only to torture people for five months. Five months is the normal lifespan and active summer season of natural locusts. God sets a definite limit on their torment, leaving room for people to recognize their misery and turn to Him in repentance.

The torment will become so painful and relentless that sufferers will actively search for death to escape their misery. Yet they will not be able to find it, for death will flee from them. God will not allow them to end their lives early to evade His righteous judgment.

John uses comparisons because these demonic figures are beyond ordinary nature. They look like horses outfitted for war, wearing what appear to be crowns of gold that show their conquering power. Their faces resemble human faces, indicating intelligence and craftiness in their attacks.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some modern writers teach that these locusts picture modern mechanized military weapons, such as attack helicopters or armored gunships.

notes.meaning: These creatures have long hair like that of women, giving them a strange and wild look. At the same time, their teeth are like the sharp teeth of lions. This shows they are ferocious and ready to tear their prey apart without mercy.

Their chests are covered with hard armor that looks like iron breastplates, making them seem invulnerable to human weapons. The sound of their wings rushing through the air is like the deafening roar of many horse-drawn war chariots charging into battle. Everything about them suggests unstoppable speed and military power.

The real weapon of these creatures is located in their tails, which carry sharp stingers like scorpions. With these tails they have the authority to inflict painful stings on mankind for five months. While their strikes produce excruciating agony, the Lord still restrains them from destroying life.

Natural locusts have no leader, but this demonic swarm is led by a king who is the angel of the bottomless pit. In Hebrew his name is Abaddon, and in Greek it is Apollyon, both meaning Destroyer. This ruler is either Satan himself or a high-ranking demonic prince who delights in tearing down God's creation.

A brief announcement marks the close of the fifth trumpet, declaring that the first woe is over. Yet there is no room for relief, because two even more dreadful woes are still on the way. Believers are encouraged to endure patiently as God's plans continue to unfold.

The sixth angel blows his trumpet, beginning the second woe. John hears a single voice coming from the four corners of the golden altar of incense before God's heavenly throne. This reminds us that God's judgments answer the cries and prayers of His suffering saints that were offered upon that very altar.

The voice directs the sixth angel to unbind the four fallen angels held at the great Euphrates River. In Old Testament history, the Euphrates marked the boundary where fierce enemies like Assyria and Babylon gathered against God's people. These demonic leaders were kept tied down until the precise hour God chose to let them loose.

The four bound angels are released right on schedule, having been kept ready for that exact hour, day, month, and year. Their mission is far more lethal than that of the locusts, because they are sent to kill a third of all mankind. This shows that even the most horrific calamities on earth occur under God's precise timing.

John is told the total count of the cavalry forces: two hundred million mounted troops. This staggering number represents an overwhelming, uncountable army far larger than any military force ever gathered by man. Most commentators understand this to picture a massive demonic army rather than human soldiers alone.

The horsemen wear armor colored fiery red, smoky blue, and yellow sulfur. The horses have terrifying heads like lions, and from their mouths pour destructive blasts of fire, smoke, and burning sulfur. These three things recall the historic destruction of Sodom and point to God's burning wrath against sin.

A full third of the human race is slaughtered by these three deadly plagues of fire, smoke, and sulfur coming from the horses' mouths. This is an immense, worldwide loss of life. Even so, God's mercy is seen in that He spares the remaining two-thirds of the world's inhabitants.

The killing power of these monstrous horses is found both in their mouths and in their tails. Their tails are like live serpents, complete with biting heads that inflict severe injury. Victims can find no safe direction, because danger attacks them from the front and strikes them from behind.

The people who survive these terrifying plagues still refuse to turn their hearts away from evil deeds. Instead, they stubbornly continue worshiping demons and bowing down to handmade idols of gold, silver, bronze, stone, and wood that cannot see, hear, or walk. Calamity alone does not soften sinful hearts when they love their false gods.

differ.view: Presbyterian and Reformed teachers point to this verse to show human depravity, arguing that terrors and judgments alone never change the human heart unless God's grace leads a person to repent.

notes.meaning: The survivors also refuse to stop their murders, witchcraft, sexual sins, and stealing. When people abandon worship of the true God, their lives naturally slide into violence, superstition, and greed. Even the horrors of hell on earth will not break the grip of sin on those who refuse God's mercy.

differ.view: Some interpreters see this failure to turn to God as proof that judgment alone cannot change the human heart, because only the saving grace of the Holy Spirit can produce true repentance.
